Wonderlands is a good Borderlands game, it could have been the BEST Borderlands game given the theme and creative freedom. Whats here is decent for a single character and playthrough, but barren of content for end game and hardcore grinders. The new additions are legitimately great, like spells replacing grenades and the freedom of character choice and skill trees at any time, but for those 2 upsides we got more 5 downsides. 

Wonderlands is generic DnD to a T. Skeletons, trolls, a mighty hero facing an evil ruler, its VERY generic given the entire theme is controlled by TINY TINA, the embodiment of a TNT stick that huffed too much glue. I was expecting more ridiculousness, the game is just the Borderlands 2 DLC up scaled to Borderlands 3 hardware with some tweeks. Thats not to say the game is bad visually or the levels are bland, i was just expecting more.

As mentioned, Wonderlands is terrible for people that want that end game grind. The top class is spore warden plus any other class, the weapons are shockingly bland and on launch has a disappointing amount of legendaries, even fewer legendaries are any good. The game also moved away from boss grinding and moved to this new "Chaos Chamber" thing. Its basically a roguelite but instead of each run being determined in the actual run, you just repeat the same levels with the same loadout against the same enemies until you find that weapon you were looking for, then its MORE boring same EVERYTHING. The Chaos Chamber has a meta, as mentioned with the top class, but in the chamber you literally NEED to run that class or you WILL die far too often. Its insane how they give us more freedom in classes but left out the most diverse thing about Borderlands, THE GUNS. 

The Majority of weapons have VERY similar stats between manufacturers, the "BAZILLION GUNS" tagline for the franchise would not work here at all. Lighting SMG is always the same, Corrosive SMG is always a laser, very few differences between weapons from the same gun maker when you hit max level and all the guns have the same level. DLC is also a MAJOR gripe i have. Instead of a traditional expansion with a new theme, they opted in for ANOTHER version of the Chaos Chamber. Instead of getting a chest, you get orbs that can be used to spin the loot wheel and you might get another bad legendary. Going back to the theme of the game, the "wonderlands" part loses its luster when you realize its generic DnD even in the DLC. So much wasted potential.

To end this review i will say some positives. The game looks great and despite the development being almost entirely during Covid lockdown, still has a great amount of side stuff and content and new ideas. The antagonist is LEAPS AND BOUNDS better than Borderlands 3's, and although this game lacks the emotional punch of the Dragon Keep DLC, its still a somewhat good story. The new additions and changes are REALLY good, the recharging spells, the multiclass system, the create-a-character is great, so many new features to the franchise work really well here. If they do turn this into a side series inbetween Borderlands releases, i would love to see each fan favorite character have their own Wonderlands. Krieg, Maya, Lilith, can even bring back Scooter and Roland. Right now, i don't regret buying the game again, and look forward to replaying it again when new content drops or updates fix some things, but the game needs a better end game and better overall expansions.

Disclaimer: Take the not-recommended with a grain of salt. I'll explain the reasons below

I would generally recommend the game in its current state, however there are some major red flags which I believe need to be addressed by Gearbox and make me question the future of the game and the companies existence to its continued support.

Positives 
Disclaimer: I'll keep these rather short, but they might help you decide

-Story is more enjoyable than bl 3 and writing has significantly improved. There are some minor annoyances with certain characters, but overall the new characters are all fairly fun and the main cast all do the job adequately
-gear progression and difficulty during the campaign is quite nice. I really disliked how bl3 showered you in loot from the get go and how common legendaries were early on. I feel like they found a much better state here where you actually can get excited by blue items all the way up to max level (if they are a good weapon type / one you enjoy)
-Effects feel nice and impactful. They did a great job on Spell Effects and Class Abilities
-The maps look amazing and the overworld adds a lot of flavor to the setting


Negatives
Disclaimer: these are a bit more extensive. Understand that some of these are personal issues based on playstyle, which may well be irrelevant to you

-Let's get the big one out of the way. The "PLCs" (dlcs) are ridiculously priced for what they are as of right now (3/4 released). DLC 3 was better, but still a long way from what we should expect from Gearbox by now. Calling them "content" is a stretch as they are basically just a few rooms of fighting with some added gimmicks. It just feels like a major waste of potential and makes me doubt the future of this game.
-Balancing is whack, both when it comes to weapons / spells as well as "classes". Especially the Spellshot gets so much from stacking a single attribute, while others just struggle to scrape enough dmg together. Spellshot literally pairs well with every other class and it speaks volumes when you actually don't even have to be spell focussed to get great benefits from using it as your second class. This issue is further amplified by ...
-The frequent increases in chaos levels (endgame system) is a major problem due to how it breaks balance over and over. When they barely started fixing chaos 35, they dropped another 15 on top leading to a state where even previously durable builds now can get health-gated by trash mobs. The absolute endgame state right now is horrendous ... it's worse than bl2 op levels imo with how few builds (mostly abusing busted interactions) can handle them.
-Chaos levels themselves. It's just not an endgame system with a lot of longevity. Too repetitive. They seem to think this alone will suffice for now, but it will just lead to burnout.
-Lack of farmable loot. Way too much of it is not farmable and the best way to acquire most pieces is to simply get lucky on world drops (i.e. back to chaos chamber). Incredibly annoying as at least for me being able to farm a weapon on the side while levelling made the replay experience of previous bl games a lot better.
-Invisible walls. Smaller issue of a bigger problem (see next points). They were incredibly lazy here imo. There are tons of invisible walls that feel like you are constantly on rails set out by the devs instead of them letting you go around exploring.
-Lack of skips / incredibly tenuous quests for replay. I've played through most of the story 3 times and let me tell you ... it's not great on new playthroughs. There are so many places you can't do anything more than wait for some dialog that you've heard 5 times before. I would have hoped they learned something from bl3 where this was also an issue. In fact, it feels deliberately designed to discourage such behaviour as there are many times you have to interact with an NPC 2-3 times in the same location. This won't allow you to run to the next place you have to go early. I understand that they want ppl to experience the quests, but rn this just cripples enjoyment for multiple playthroughs. It also adds to the "on-rails" experience mentioned when it came to invisible walls.
-Classes are weird rn. There is less build diversity than bl 3 due to the limited skill trees and that most class combos can do 1 (or 2 at most) builds between them (some have almost no synergy of course). Additionally, a lot of the information is still obfuscated as always (which types are additive, which multiplicative) and a lot of nodes feel meaningless (significantly more so than they did in bl3). I reckon the last point is down to the additional attributes we get from rings and amulet this time around, but let me tell you. Speccing points, especially early, never felt so unsatisfying in bl before.

Pweh that's it. I have a lot of fun with the game right now, but there are some major issues the game has right now (both design and balance-wise). I would recommend it only if you know you enjoy this type of game and you aren't someone who cares about targeted farming and "speed-running" when playing.

So, I will preface all of this by saying that I went into this game with low expectations. The Borderlands games were an absolute favorite of mine for the first and second games, but by the time The Pre-Sequel and 3 came out (I forget which order they were released in, I want to say Pre-Sequel was released first) I had pretty much lost interest in the franchise and really FPS games entirely, but when I saw Tiny Tina's my inner RPG addict tag teamed with my nostalgia and convinced me to buy the game after I had beaten Elden Ring for the nth time and was in desperate search of something new. 

[hr][/hr]

[h1][u][b]The Pros[/b][/u][/h1]

○ [u]Classic Borderlands[/u] 
And I do mean classic. It felt like playing the original game again. No grand universe-scope plot. Just you as some random nobody going around and beating up on crap until it spits out loot and gold...so much gold!

○ [u]The Comedic Value[/u] 
This was one of the many things I loved about the original game. Is the humor brash and juvenile? Absolutely. But it's part of what makes the game so unique. I love it.

○ [u]What RPG elements were in the game, were solid[/u] 
I liked the class mechanics (I've only done Gloombringer (Graveborn/Clawbringer) so far, but I fully intend to give the other classes a test run). The action skills were cool, I really dug the talent trees and the way the different class combos could play off of each other.

○ [u]The utter disregard for the Fourth Wall[/u] 
Okay. So, I'm a writer. This is one of my favorite literary devices of all time. That direct split where the fourth wall comes down and the characters in the story are [b]fully[/b] aware that they're fictional characters is just...yes. I loved it.

○ [u]Tina, Valentine, and Fette[/u] 
The dynamic between these three was just fantastic. They really brought the game together, and Andy Samburg's performance as Valentine was A plus.

○ [u]Claptrap[/u]
Seeing this little guy pop up at various points was a really nice dose of nostalgia. I don't really have much else to say than that without risking spoiling anything, but thank you Gearbox for bringing him into the fold for this one.

○ [u]The Story[/u]
Once again, Gearbox managed to do what so few FPS games have been able to manage in the past. We got a compelling narrative alongside great gunplay. I was invested in the story, I wanted to know what was going to happen next. I even went as far as loading an outdated cloud save when my computer decided to seize up right before a cutscene.

○ [u]The Atmosphere[/u]
I have to admit, this impressed me [i]a lot[/i]. Gearbox managed to encapsulate what it's like to sit at a TTRPG session with an absolute loon of a DM (love you Tina, but you're off your rocker and that's what I love most about you). The bickering between Valentine and Fette, as well as two of them regularly poking holes in Tina's prepared content that resulted in her having to improvise like hell. It was great. It brought back some fond memories from a campaign I ran years ago.

[hr][/hr]

[h1][u][b]The Cons[/b][/u][/h1]

○ [u]I felt a little...misled[/u] 
This is probably my own fault because truth be told, I knew [i]nothing[/i] about this game aside from the vague explanation of "It's Borderlands meets D&D." I went into it expecting more RPG elements than it had, something with more focus on sword and board and less guns. But, again. I think I did that one to myself. 

○ [u]The guns[/u] 
So, as we all know from our time spent playing Borderlands (and if you don't know, then now you will), one of the big themes in all the games was the whole "every gun manufacturer has their own gimmick" deal. I feel like I get what Gearbox was trying to do here, that is to blend magic into modern/futuristic firearms, but in my opinion it just fell short. 

In the 40 hours or so it took me to work my way to the end of the game whilst being distracted by side quests, I found myself almost always holding onto a Blackpowder weapon that was a huge item level gap behind other options because there wasn't some gimmick to it. It was just a gun.

○ [u]The Character Customization[/u]

Okay, I want to preface this with one very important thing. To my knowledge, Gearbox has never given us any sort of customization options besides color (I think that was a thing, that might not even have been) in any of the previous games, so I applaud them for finally doing so. 

That being said, I found the whole system utterly clunky and annoying. The initial character creation had so few options, I finally ended up just randomizing things because even with the slider overdrive on there just was not enough diversity of options to really compel me to sit there on character creation for hours on end like I've done with many RPG titles in the past.

○ [u]The Overworld[/u]

I felt like I needed a map to read what was essentially the world map. The Overworld, to me, felt like an unnecessary mini game and a pretty perfunctory attempt at giving that open world feel to a game franchise that has traditionally been pretty linear. The shrine piece collecting was tiresome considering the limited reward for finishing each of them, and the side quests were almost without exception nothing more than the same fetch quest with different flavor text.

○[u]The Spells[/u]

The only reason I found myself actually using spells was because of the Graveborn talent that granted HP regen on spell use and Morhaim's Blessing which gave you all of those wonderful kill skills every time you activated a spell. They were a utility item for me, half the time I didn't even bother to aim them I just tapped the button to gain the bonuses it would bring. I feel like more could have been done here.

○ [u]Performance Issues[/u]

Specs for the PC I played on
◘ Intel i5 9400F 2.90GHz
◘ 8GB DDR4 RAM
◘ NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 SUPER
◘ Game data stored on HDD (not 100% sure on speed, but I think 7200)

For starters, I want to state clearly that I am completely aware that I am barely above the minimum requirements to run the game. This is a hand-me-down PC that I'm still working on getting new parts for.

That being said, I ran into [i]constant[/i] crashes when I first started playing, and this was with the game's settings set as low as they could go. There was stuttering, and freezing, and all sorts of crazy stuff. I ended up having to go into NVIDIA's control panel and fiddle with some rendering settings just to get the game stable. 

Vsync was not an option for me, much to my chagrin (motion sickness issues), but I believe this is a me problem given the strain that vSync puts on the GPU and my GPU's inability to handle it.

Cutscenes were also still a pretty big problem even after my fiddling in the NVIDIA control panel. I had to cut power to the machine via the power supply switch at one point because a cutscene locked my computer up to the point where even holding the power button down wouldn't send a shutdown command.

[hr][/hr]

[h1][b][u]To Summarize: A solid 8/10 from me[/u][/b][/h1]

Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is a First Person Shooter set in the Borderlands universe, where the player is taking part in a Dungeons & Dragons style Bunkers & Badasses campaign run by Tina.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

•	Its Borderlands with a fantasy theme, so if you’ve played any Borderlands shooter, the combat will feel familiar.

•	Fight against skeletons, goblins, giant crabs, shark dogs and nagas. Borderlands has always featured strange creatures, so the fantasy theme basically just means “no robots”.

•	There are a few character classes to choose from. I started with Clawbringer, who reminded me of Marvel’s Thor because they can throw a massive hammer to deal lightning (or fire) damage to all enemies in a large area. I also had a pet wyvern who flies around breathing fire at enemies. Part way through the game you can multiclass, and I chose Spore Warden to get a pet mushroom who runs around biting enemies. Those pets are surprisingly useful and got quite a few kills as well as just generally distracting enemies.

•	As usual you can equip a variety of pistols, SMGs, assault rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, and rocket launchers, which all have different magazine sizes, zoom sights, elemental damage, etc. You can also use spells, which are just fantasy themed grenades, and melee weapons.

•	The best part of the game is the unique gun designs, which are a lot of fun to use. There were so many times that I decided “this is my new favourite gun”, only to find something else that was even better a short time later.  A few of my favourites include an SMG which freezes enemies, a sniper rifle that shoots triple saw blades, a crossbow that fires crossbows (which fire extra bolts), an SMG which fires a poison damage laser beam that slightly homes in on nearby enemies, and a rapid fire pistol which halved my health when reloading but leeched health back when damaging enemies.

•	The hard / “intense” difficulty started out fairly challenging, but over time became easier as I found more powerful guns.

[h1]Story[/h1]

•	Both the main story and all the side quests are absolute nonsense. Dialogue is terrible. Every character is annoying. Because Tina is the DM, everything sounds like it was written by her. In previous Borderlands games, when Tina shows up for a couple of quests, her chaotic energy can be an interesting change of pace. But it turns out that a whole game that sounds like Tina is just exhausting. After a few hours I lost interest and stopped listening as much as possible.

[h1]Technical[/h1]

•	It took me 29 hours to complete the main story and most of the side quests.

•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is a decent game if you just want to turn off your brain and shoot stuff. Buy on sale.

This game isn't amazing but it is def worth a try if you like the borderlands series, especially when on sale. 

If you go in with reasonable expectations (I believe I did) then its pretty fun. 

The gameplay is actually pretty engaging, it starts off kind of slow as expected but quickly picks up. The class progression is nice and the skills seem meaningful, giving substantial bonuses (at least the classes I chose). In previous games some skills didn't feel like they did much besides have a place in the tree. I like the stat allocation system as well, I think this should be brought back in the future. 

The loot dice are a good system and overall I enjoyed the collectibles, they were placed in fun and creative ways where it felt rewarding to explore and not as if were just aimlessly running around until you spotted one. 

Something I thought was great was they didn't build the game around being replayed a few times. You finish the game at max level. It feels less tedious and not as boring when you aren't doing the same quests multiple times.

The overworld JRPG system was kind of cool, it works well for this game but I'm not sure about for future BORDERLANDS games. I did like vehicles in previous games but they were also kind of a hassle. The JRPG system made it so maps were more compact, it felt better designed and meaningful. I think borderlands wouldn't be the same without vehicles but wonderlands does a good job without them. The fast travel system was GREAT, being able to fast travel from anywhere is amazing and should be in all borderlands games to come.

I liked the chaos chamber, its a good endgame system to get good loot and expands well on the arenas you find in the overworld. I do think they should make it more roguelike-like, the replayability wasn't amazing. I hope they bring it back and improve upon it in the future.

The overall story was decent as well, I liked the ending but was kind of bored of it halfway through. Kind of felt like they just stitched the beginning and end together. 

I will say I bought the chaotic great edition (the one that includes the season pass) and I don't think the DLC is worth it unless you get it for the discounted price, and even then its not that great. The only thing going for it is a few new areas to explore that aren't very different from those in the base game besides aesthetic. They are more like long side quests than actual DLC. The class that you get from the DLC is fun but otherwise I'd save your money.

The setting may be fantasy, but it’s still Borderlands. Which means you’ll be collecting a lot of randomly generated guns and comparing stats. Some are going to have aspects that aren’t clear until you try and use them, like bad sights, or excessive recoil, or a weird shot pattern that makes them useless at anything but short range or against huge targets.

There are 6 character classes, plus one unlocked via DLC. Each only has one skill tree, where prior games had 3, but you eventually get to choose an additional class, so there’s a wide variety of mix-and-match. Skill effects are very gradual, so it takes a lot of progression down a tree before the class feels at all different from the generic shooting that all classes do.

In addition to guns, there are spells. Which feel like the guns with the various random attributes, though some do things that guns don’t, like spawn hydra heads that act like turrets. Some classes do better with spells than others.

The fantasy setting means the environments are much more varied than the typical Borderlands game. There are several large zones, and they’re all maze-like enough that they’re confusing to navigate, even while referencing the map.

There are a bunch of smaller maps for random encounters / pocket dungeons. Most are like Doom-style death match arenas, moderately complex rather than the simple open spaces of arenas in older Borderlands games, but still somewhat smalll overall.

Combat balance isn’t really to my liking. Lots of enemies like to close to melee range, and a fair number of the later game enemies can teleport to do so. Random encounters / pocket dungeons will outright spawn enemies behind you. This makes the game chaotic rather than tactical, it’s often a matter of holing up in a corner and shooting enemies as they charge, or running around like mad. 

Not once did I find a situation where using a rocket launcher made sense. I used spells for big area of effect attacks, because I could have both a spell and a regular, fast-firing single target gun equipped at the same time.

I enjoyed the side-quests a lot more than the main story. The conceit is that it’s a tabletop RPG with a manic 13 year old as a game master, so everything is intentionally silly and juvenile. This works for the side quests that are generally pop-culture parodies of games and movies, but it also means the main quest feels pretty shallow.

One aspect of the main quest I really disliked was that the main villain has a mind of his own, and is rebelling against Tina as game master. Which doesn’t make any sense, really, and his complaints about her “tyranny” ring hollow, since it’s explicitly a game. I think Wonderlands would have been better, overall, if they’d skipped that and stuck with the idea that he’s an NPC played by Tina, like the rest of the major NPCs.

Overall, it’s pretty good. It took me a while to warm to it at first, but eventually I adapted to the vibe.

This game is a joy.  But I know I feel that way because I am both a huge Borderlands nerd and a huge Dungeons & Dragons nerd.  If you are not also both of these things, this one might not be for you.

Being just a Borderlands fan isn't quite enough, because there's not a lot of Borderlands here, especially not at the beginning.  Don't get me wrong, the gameplay is peak Gearbox shlooter, but aside from that, the art style, Tina's narration, and a few cameos, this game doesn't appear to have strong links with the Borderlands universe.    

I think Dragon Keep resonated with folks because it was Dungeons & Dragons but it was ALSO Borderlands, and Wonderlands doesn't find that balance.  I'm not even sure it tries.

Did you notice Wonderlands is rated T rather than M?  That is not a fluke.  The familiar sense of humor is there, but this is the questionable taste of Borderlands filtered through the mind and habits of a childlike teenager.  It's a kinder, gentler 'Lands, targeted to a younger audience.

And that brings me to a point that I haven't seen a bunch of folks acknowledge: this is clearly not a Borderlands spinoff, but the tentative launch of a new franchise for Gearbox.  And I say that because it explains a lot about what I'm seeing.  The game is big, beautiful, and fun, but it is not the polished experience that Borderlands 3 was.  

Overall, the UX is far clunkier, and reminds me more of Borderlands 2 than the third game.  In some places this looks like the franchise trying to find its own feel, and in others it looks like a development team unwilling to spend big or take risks on a new IP.  This would also illustrate why the DLC on offer is so minimal -- Gearbox couldn't be sure this dragon was going to fly, and rightly so.

There are some great additions, too: the ability to Town Portal, Diablo-style, is something Borderlands has always lacked, and it is welcome.  The overworld is more interesting than the classic map screen.  The character generator is fantastic (why don't more games give you the ability to turn "slider overdrive" on and off?!), and the thrill of unlocking new cosmetic options through play and lucky drops is enjoyable enough that I'm not even mad about having to unlock new cosmetic options through play and lucky drops.  

Those same cosmetic options also now sell for a hefty price, unlike in BL3 where they were all only worth $1, so finding one is always welcome, even when you pull one you've already unlocked.

As for the Dungeons & Dragons (or Bunkers & Badasses, I suppose) side of things, I think the best way to describe my experience is that yes, I've heard all these jokes before, but never told quite so well.  Borderlands has always traded heavily in familiarity, and Wonderlands is no different, although the source material may have changed.  

Many events in Wonderlands are punctuated with the sound of dice being rolled, and it warms my heart every time.  There's a lot of love here, and it makes for an enjoyable experience.  I respect the hell out of that even if it isn't particularly original.

We've all had chocolate chip cookies before.  It doesn't stop us wanting more chocolate chip cookies, particularly if they're well made.  If I am slightly underwhelmed by Wonderlands on the whole, I have great hopes and expectations for Wonderlands II.

[code]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is a Borderlands spin-off that’s just … fine. It offers exactly what one would expect from a Borderlands game at this point but also doesn’t manage to reach the heights of some of its predecessors or even surpass them - making the final product tough to recommend at full price[/code]

When [i]Tiny Tina’s Assault on Dragon Keep [/i] released as a DLC for [i]Borderlands 2[/i], it was widely praised for its unexpectedly well-working mix of [i]Borderlands[/i] gameplay and a “Dungeons & Dragons” fantasy setting, now called “Bunkers & Badasses”. Not only did it offer riffs on genre-typical tropes and popular fantasy works but it also managed to tell a surprisingly emotional story about dealing with the loss of a loved one. Even today, it’s often referenced as one of the best DLC out there.

As such, it’s almost surprising that it took almost ten years for the “Bunkers & Badasses” setting to return to the Borderlands once more - only this time as a full-fledged spin-off. But as the latest game in the franchise after the disappointing [i]Borderlands 3[/i], can [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] live up to the DLC that inspired it?

The answer to that question isn’t “yes”, sure, but it’s also not a profound “no”. [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] does quite a few things right but after the mere 22 hours it took me to complete all main quests, side quests, dungeons and shrines of the main game, I got mixed feelings about what’s on offer here - at least for its full price.

Let’s take the gameplay, for example. [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] takes the [i]Borderlands[/i] looter-shooter formula and once again transfers it into a realm of fantasy. However, in contrast to the original DLC, we finally got ‘proper’ fantasy characters to play as, as well as associated weapons like a shotgun firing arrows or an SMG with magic beams. Grenades have been replaced by magic spells, which are way more fun, and we even got melee weapons now, a more than welcome change from the basic punching we got before.The new classes & skills are also great, even allowing for two-class combinations!

If we combine these additions with a lot of enemies, levelling & loot (of course), the basic gameplay loop works just as it always did, if not better. The new additions are fun to use in practice and even though I’d have loved more enemy variety, it’s equally fun to shoot skeletons and wyverns here as it was shooting skags or Psychos in [i]Borderlands[/i] games before. That said, this unfortunately isn’t the case all the time, thanks to a few issues.

One of these issues concerns the early game. Simply put, during the first few hours of my playthrough, I was usually stuck with (lower rarity) guns that just didn’t feel great to use. It was not until later that shooting enemies in the face actually started to be fun. Sure, one should not expect the most powerful weapons at the start of the game – but at least give me something that feels nice to use. However, to be fair here: This could’ve been an issue that was simply caused by bad loot luck (which, by the way, is a stat that can be increased by finding lucky dice hidden all over the world). However, I can’t recall having similar experiences with the other [i]Borderlands[/i] games.

Another problem is (item) progression, which wasn’t as consistent/smooth as I’d liked it to be. For example, I once got a gun drop that had significant higher item level (~500) than any of my other guns (~400) at the time - a lucky find, sure, but it took hours until other loot drops caught up to that one lucky find in terms of item level. This also caused issues in terms of difficulty, as sometimes my high item level weapons essentially tore through enemy encounters while I sometimes felt like I was underperforming even though my item level was perfectly matching the typical loot I got.

The last gameplay-related issue I want to talk about concerns side content and to some degree, the endgame of [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i]. First of, the explorable zones aren’t connected with each other anymore like in previous [i]Borderlands[/i] games. Instead, we got a tabletop-style overworld, so the player(s) can pick each zone/dungeon/quest/etc. as they want. In my opinion, this makes world feel rather disjointed in my opinion, but it does fit the “Bunkers & Badasses” theme.

What I actually want to criticize here is how much of the side content in [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] just turns out to be random fights in the few same small areas/arenas. A lot of side activities (certain side quests, camps, random encounters, dungeons, mines, etc.) just throw you into the same few maps where you’re doing nothing but fighting a random bunch of enemies until you’re allowed to move on. Even the endgame, consisting of the so-called “chaos chamber”, is basically just this with a bunch of shallow rogue-like mechanics on top of it. These same-y encounters basically feel like filler of which I quickly grew tired of. I would’ve vastly preferred more “traditional” side quests instead.

In terms of writing, [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] is as much of a mixed experience as the gameplay was. The good news here is that the main story doesn’t reach the lows of a [i]Borderlands 3[/i] and does a good job of getting the player through the various areas of the game. It should also be noted that thanks to its spin-off nature, it’s also completely accessible for newcomers to the franchise – no previous knowledge required.

That said, being a spin-off makes [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] a double-edged sword for longtime fans of the franchise as there are only extremely few connections to the remaining [i]Borderlands[/i] franchise. [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] is all about its own original characters instead, so don’t expect a cameo-filled fantasy adventure here.

The writing of [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] offers the commentary on the fantasy genre you’d expect if you played the [i]Borderlands 2[/i] DLC. Or any [i]Borderlands[/i] game, really. While much of it fell flat for me personally, by being too on-the-nose for example (stuff like a quest chain parodying “The Witcher” called “The Ditcher”), the game did get a laugh out of me on a few occasions. Considering how the game loves to reference current internet culture (like an angry customer called “Karen”), however, I’m not sure how well some of it may age.

As for the story itself, again, iit serves its purpose just fine - but doesn’t leave much of a lasting impression beyond that. A villain rebelling against the game master sounds like a fun idea but isn’t really explored much – just like the villain itself. The other “Bunker & Badasses” players are nothing more than one-dimensional characters representing tabletop player stereotypes. The game also misses the emotional connection the original DLC had, which elevated it from being a simple parody to something greater. 

That said, the story did offer some unexpectedly hilarious moments (which I won’t spoiler here) and it doesn’t overstay its welcome. In short, if you’re just looking for a game that doesn't take itself too seriously or if you’re a big fan of the fantasy genre who loves some good ol’ references, you’re in luck. If you’re a [i]Borderlands[/i] fan hoping for some revelations or another emotional journey however, you might need to adjust your expectations.

I also need to mention some technical problems I experienced during my playthrough (mainly audio issues, NPCs being stuck in animation loops, game crashing).

To conclude, [i]Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands[/i] does some things right - and some wrong. Sometimes, with the right guns and skills, it felt amazing to blast through enemies. Sometimes, as I was working through monotonous battles, I was wondering if I should just drop the whole game. Quite similar to a real tabletop session, really. Regardless, it’s a game that should not be bought at full price - I'd advise waiting for a significant sale instead.

I picked up this game because Tiny Tina's Assault was a masterpiece, and I've wanted a full game version of that for YEARS. This... This isn't it. The D&D based mechanics are fun and sparkly at first, and that alone kept me playing a lot longer than it should have. The emotion, the humor, the purpose, everything that made the DLC so special is spectacularly missing from this.

Everything in the game is filtered to be "age appropriate" for younger audiences, which effectively destroys almost everything that made Borderlands, well Borderlands, but also removes like 80% of Tina's personality. She's no longer the traumatized, deranged little maniac in a cute basket crumpets. She's just a normal, "quirky" teen girl. She's still cute, but everything that made her a precious bean that needed to be cared for (and provided therapy) is just gone. It's like taking OG Harley Quinn and turning her into an innocent chibi, still nice but not really special anymore.

Tina wasn't the only thing damaged by this either. The side quests are dull, combat is tedious to the point I just run straight through any unscripted fights now. The "big baddies" are waaayyy to easy to fight. The weapons are all the same [i] just in different font [/i], to the point that I don't think I've swapped anything in my loadout for at least 15 in-game hours. I hardly even pick anything off the ground anymore.

I tried so hard to love this game. Some of the mainline story is really cute and fun, and playing a character with 2 summons has been pretty neat (even if it's just the mechromancer with more fairy dust and friendship). Exploring the overlands could probably be considered a game in of itself. On a really good day, if I'm not thinking about it, I might tell you that this is the best game I've played in a couple years. That's just the Tina fangirl playing a game of denial though. The reality is if I stop to really think about my experience playing this game in comparison to the DLC that made me want it, everything just looks so lackluster and leaves me feeling mislead. 

I would still probably recommend this to preteens that want an entry to Borderlands, or maybe for people who don't particularly care about Tiny Tina and just want another Borderlands style game to occupy them for a while. For those who absolutely adored dragons keep or prefer the more traditional Borderlands experience though, don't bother. You're not the target audience. It's not worth the money.

If you think I'm being overly critical (fair enough) and still want to play, at [i] least [/i] buy it on sale.

Tina's Wonderlands; A game that, despite my hours, I am still quite mixed on. 
Most of my issues with the game come from the writing, main story especially. Where characters feel like caricatures, either flanderised or just one-note. The main story itself doesn't go too far either, opting to stay completely safe to the entire franchise rather than do anything actually interesting. Tina isn't really Tina anymore, but the safe and wacky version of Tina with little to no issues aside from maybe a few quests.

For main story conflict, there is little to none (aside from a few main issues that get resolved almost instantly) and the universe itself doesn't actually make sense. Things happen in-game independent of the DM and characters outside of the game, which then affect the outside world, rather than the other way around. 
Also, Tina is still 12/13 in this game and will occasionally make inappropriate jokes. There were maybe 3 or 4, but, those times were just uncomfortable and definitely not as tasteful as the game seems to play them off as. 

The humour in this entry feels like it changed a lot, which makes sense considering the best head writer in the series hasn't been here since Borderlands 2. So we're stuck with reddit-tier or below-reddit tier jokes. Find them funny if you wish, but it is incredibly low effort in terms of writing. With the slap in the face being how safe it plays every single joke, considering one of the main draws of Borderlands used to be how messed up the world was while being so lighthearted. This is just light-hearted without the reality to it.

However, and the biggest however possible -- if you can get past the writing or just mute while playing, the actual gunplay itself and how classes work feels phenomenal. As of Chapter 4, you unlock multiclassing which opens you up to just over 20 combinations of classes that can let you play the game whichever way you wish. My only criticism with multiclassing is the fact that the game doesn't give you your secondary class sheet upon choosing, and, you can only switch second classes at the end of the game. 

But that is the reason I played through this game so many times (and will likely play through more in the future), because of how effective the skills, spells, guns and classes work in tandem with each other. I was quite surprised, since, I really thought I wouldn't like this game from the story alone. I'm glad I stuck through it.

Another side note, for people who do care about postgame, the most fun you'll be having is save editing on your own or messing around with the game of your own accord. Since, the only post-game is the Chaos Chamber, and you have to save edit for anything close to the replayability of the TVHM seen in other previous games. The modding "community" isn't as strong as BL3 and especially not BL2, though I can't remove points on this game for it I feel the need to point it out for anyone looking to mod the game like BL3/BL2.

Get it on sale for sure (considering the price, and the lack of content compared to similar priced games of the series), and avoid the short cashgrab DLC's -- unless you're just getting Shattering Spectreglass for the Blightcaller class, because that was the only highlight of the entire extra amount of money I spent on said DLC. I'm sure you can look through the DLCs for yourself to realise why people don't like them, but all they really do is add more chaos chamber content at the end of the day and not a whole lot of it.
And if you don't like the writing, take a speedrun tip and exit to main menu whenever a character talks for too long. Works most of the time for skipping dialogue.

Okay, long time Borderlands fan here. I've put over 200 hours into this game on PS5 and completed the main story three times, so I know the story and the end game pretty well. Let me start this review by saying the base game here is really good. The game play and the story are both great - aside from the odd story character I found to be weirdly handled...

The story is several steps up from that mess in BL3. Is it on par with BL2? I wouldn't say so, but it's still great in its own right. Definitely a worthy continuation of the Dragon's Keep DLC. The main bad guy is surprisingly well set up. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone that played BL2 and the Dragon's Keep DLC just for the story.

The game play is very similar to BL3, in all the right ways in my opinion. The movement feels good, not like the awkward rigid movement in BL2, and the new spell system makes for a lot of fun. Spells replace grenades in this game, so while you technically have infinite ammo, you are restricted by the cool down (in most cases) so you can't spam all your grenades/spells to instantly clear a zone. The spells do make for much more varied play styles though, so I think they're a great addition.

Playable characters now have voice lines and actually interact with the world in unique and interesting ways depending on your character's personality. The character customisation here is far better than any BL game previously, and offers a respectable level of customisation. My only wish would be the ability to transmog armour. Armour replaces Class Mods from previous BL games, Amulets replace Relics/Artifacts, and new Rings (you can equip up to two) also act like additional Relics/Artifacts. This is a decent change, and makes sense. Wards also replace shields, and function exactly the same as shields from BL3, for example. I like all of these changes.

I also like the new hero point and myth rank systems. Hero points are like additional skill points you can use to increase crit damage, crit chance, spell cooldown, etc. Myth rank is basically like BAR from BL2. Both are great. The level cap is currently 40, so a little lower than the max level of 50 in BL2's base game. Although you do unlock your action skill at level two, so you don't lose out on as many points as you'd expect. I expect this to get increased in future though.

The actual classes you can choose, however, leave something to be desired. Currently, the Spellshot is by far the most powerful class, and there's not really much point going with anything else. Spellshot + Stabbomancer seems to be the meta for most end game builds, and it's easy to see why. It would be nice if the other classes got some buffs to put them on par, or at least close to, the power of the Spellshot - in their own respective ways (I'm not saying Clawbringer should be able to deal as much spell damage as the Spellshot, for example).

The new split class system is also a bit of a double edged sword too, I think. On one hand, it means players only have to level up half as many characters, which is great for more casual players that want to try every character. On the other hand, it makes which class you choose less impactful since their short comings can be offset by choosing an appropriate secondary class. Moreover, combining two classes which compliment each other in unique ways makes for an unbalanced end game - like Spellshot + Stabbomancer using Double Knot and From The Shadows. More character balance is definitely needed in my opinion.

The guns also leave something to be desired. The vast majority of legendary weapons feel underwhelming, in terms of damage dealt, special effects, and cool factor. BL2 and 3 had some awesome legendaries... The Monarch/Dictator, Unkempt Harold, Slagga, Conference Call, etc. This game doesn't have anything that comes even close to any of those. In fact, a lot of regular (i.e. non-unique) blue/purple weapons outperform many legendaries. That should not be the case. This is made worse by the fact that legendaries are rarer in this game compared to BL3 (although more common than in BL2). So getting legendaries is harder than in BL3, and they also perform worse. That doesn't make for a fun game play experience.

Melee weapons have also been added to this game, and they actually add a lot to the experience. Legendary melee weapons (unlike the majority of legendary guns) offer really cool benefits over their lesser rarity counterparts, and can change how you play the game. This is a really fun change. However, don't expect to be running any melee only builds because there are a lot of flying enemies you can't melee - plus a lot of bosses that also can't be melee'd (like... why?). That being said, I'm glad they're in the game, even if the developers seem to forget that sometimes when they're designing bosses.

The end game consists of Chaos Chambers - dungeon style encounters which allow you to unlock Chaos Levels (mayhem levels from BL3). This is actually pretty fun at first, but due to lack of variety, tedious farming in the final loot chamber, and over reliance on farming Chaos Chambers for loot, they quickly become uninteresting. Spending 15 minutes doing a run and then another 15 minutes (or probably more) sorting through loot in the final loot room is not my idea of a fun time. They have made efforts to improve this experience by adding vending machines in the final room, but it still feels like a chore to slog through a Chaos Chamber. This is made worse by the fact that they keep raising the maximum Chaos level. I thought 20 was fine. It was pretty hard, but not punishing. Then they upped it to 35, and destroyed build diversity because it was so difficult. Now it's 50. I haven't taken the time to get to Chaos Level 50, but I don't imagine it's going to be fun. There are now more Chaos levels than actual levels... And you don't get skill points for increasing your Chaos level. You don't get anything. You get tougher enemies and a chance for slightly more powerful loot to drop in the form of Chaotic/Volatile/Primordial/Ascended loot. Great...

Now for my biggest gripe with this game - aside from the current state of Chaos Chambers. The "first season pass." Firstly, I find the idea of a game having multiple season passes offensive already. Was my £55 initial payment not enough? You need another £50 in the form of two additional season passes? Really? Insulting... Not to mention the fact that the first DLC came out less than a month after the release of the actual game, so they were surely working on it before the game was released and decided not to include it in the base game... and it came out with bugs which they only just recently fixed by the way (shark enemies with missing names, for example). This whole things stinks of corporate greed, and I hate it. As for the DLCs themselves, well, they're trash. They're basically just additional Chaos Chambers you pay extra for. Yes, it's pretty nice that once you complete one of these DLCs their rooms and bosses get added to the Chaos Chamber rotation, but they're still ultimately more monotonous Chaos Chambers.

Why no story DLCs? BL2 had some of the best story DLCs ever. This game is literally a spin off from one of BL2's DLCs. It seems like after BL2 you guys forgot how to make good DLC. BL3 had a similar problem with seemingly lazy DLC content churned out. The only reason to buy any BL3 or Wonderlands DLCs is for the powerful loot you guys put in them. Other than that, they hardly deserve to see the light of day, never mind the hard earned money from your player base. It's frankly insulting. And what makes it even worse in this case (compared to BL3) is there's no transparency. TALK TO YOUR PLAYERS. Leaving us in the dark is just disrespectful.

In summary, I would recommend playing this game if you liked Dragon's Keep or BL3. Wait for a decent sale (<=£30) and buy the base game. Avoid the first season pass for now, it's nowhere near worth it.

This installment made it nearly unplayable for us due to one significant change from the other games in this series: players earn more experience points (EP) for delivering the finishing blow. Over time, the level/EP disparity between my wife and me grew so substantial that I had to intentionally hold back, which reduced my enjoyment. From levels 10 to 40, I found myself merely running into every battle, hoping my pet wouldn't defeat the enemies, and allowing my wife to finish them off. It became incredibly frustrating to just watch her engage in combat while I still had a considerable EP lead, regardless of our efforts to balance it. My uncontrollable pet often dealt the killing blows, and my main objective became avoiding enemy kills. The thrill of acquiring and using powerful weapons vanished because what was the point? I constantly felt unsatisfied and powerless.

Why introduce such a mechanic in co-op? It would be more suitable for a "competition" mode or something similar. Co-op players should have the freedom to choose whether they want a level difference or not.

Overall, it was a disheartening experience. The only solace came from the humorous dialogues between battles. Each encounter was pure frustration, and we won't be revisiting this game. For context, we've replayed BL1, 2, Pre-Sequel, and 3 multiple times, amassing over 3,000 hours of gameplay combined.

Very disapointing!!!

PS: Yes, we googled and tried a lot of things to get rid of the EP difference. But after 2-3 fights I had (thanks to the pet) again an enormous EP advantage!

I honestly wanted to give this game a negative recommendation after I finished the main story last year. I've since reloaded my save and played the post-game and I had a few realizations that swayed my opinion.

Let me get this out of the way: the main story content is awful. It's cheesy, cringey, and too childish in a lot of places. The idea in its core is cool and unique, and the antagonist is great. But the execution and especially writing could be so much better. The side quests are not much of an improvement, with most of them being either forgettable or similarly cheesy.

The dice system is a good idea on paper, and they're fun to collect. My main issue with it is that the dice themselves are so unrewarding once you do get them. You can get an amazing roll and still only get a blue. Matter of fact, the loot in this game is awful when compared to BL2's and especially BL3's. You're literally 80% of your way through the game and you still get whites and greens. Item management is also a nightmare, with it being harder then ever to determine which loot is better than the other.

I do also have some minor issues, like a lot of the bosses being either too easy (the cthulhu boss) or one-shotting you out of nowhere (the ice skeleton boss). I also wish the game pushed its fantasy theme more rather than just being another Borderlands game but with spells as grenades.

What changed my mind with the game are a few things. Once you get near the end, you do get hooked into the story and it ends in a somewhat satisfactory way. You also start to get purples regularly as you reach the end, which are fun to use and essentially "activate" your build. Speaking of which, the skill trees and character building in this game is just as good if not better than BL3's. I did also have fun with the spells, even if you do end up trashing 99% of them. The Chaos Chambers are also really fun. In fact, this is the first time that I actually wanted to engage with a Borderlands game's end-game content.

I do wish that the game received a few more patches before it was abandoned. It's a good but flawed experience.

If not, skip this and play literally any of the other Borderlands games. Don't be fooled by the fantasy-theme, this is just a Borderlands-game with a fantasy coat of paint - it's still a looter [i]shooter[/i].

Before a sucka rolls for initiative, said sucka must know that Gearbox has been on a quest to rebottle the magic they unleashed with Borderlands 2. So naturally they would want to replicate the best DLC from B2 because usually, the DLC is the best part of Borderlands. This game breaks that tradition spectacularly, so don’t waste your money on the season pass. As for living up to Borderlands 2, Wonderlands doesn’t get them quite there but it’s certainly a better attempt than Pre-Sequel and B3. 

The core gameplay of looting and shooting doesn’t stray far at all though some of the names and means have changed and it’s all less flashy and seizure inducing. There are fewer traditional Borderlands maps but they are all very different from one another in theme and play. The maps are also definitely smaller but all you’re missing there is the annoying borderlands driving gameplay which is a little like driving the world's most unsatisfying bumper car. All that’s been replaced with a tabletop overworld and the good ol’ fast travel which is more convenient than ever. So it’s like you’re getting half of the movie Julie and Julia but only the half with Merril Streep.

Besides the traditional maps we are used to, there are arena-battle-like encounters which pop up with both random encounters and the smaller dungeons on the overworld. They are fun and action packed but a bit overused and there aren’t enough minimaps in the rotation so it gets a little tiring. So I do recommend Tiny Tina Wonderlands for anyone who enjoyed Tiny Tina’s Assault on Dragon Keep but the DLC for Wonderlands isn’t the desert at the end of a good meal, it’s the kernels at the bottom of your bucket of popcorn.

[i]Tiny Tina's Wonderlands[/i] does some new unique things that are interesting and enjoyable, but also offers far less than any Borderlands games and is the laziest Gearbox has ever been with content. They play really hard into this D&D parody, which creates a cool class system with multiple class abilities, and the freedom to multi-class / spec points into two different classes at once. I thought this allowed for some pretty unique builds compared to other Borderlands games; my build heavily favored and amplified specific types of elemental damage including kill skills that would further benefit me. On the flip side, the D&D parody in many ways hurts the story of the game, as Tina is essentially serving as your DM. This gives the story a playful nature, but I honestly felt like creativity was lost because of this, the Borderlands world is already very unique and has a weird variety of locations and enemies. While the environment design/art teams undoubtedly cooked at times the enemy variety is the worst it has ever been. 

A large amount of the game's content is really lazy. Between locations you navigate an overworld map where enemies can spawn and engage you in combat scenarios. These might as well be AI generated and are easily the worst part of the game. You spawn into a map and have to defeat a certain amount of enemies before it ends, gives you a few items, and boots you back to the overworld. These encounters are so repetitive and boring, and the enemies don't spawn all at once so you'll often need to find one that's hiding on the other side of the map, hunt it down, kill it, and then repeat with two more waves of enemies. While the overworld encounters are avoidable, about 25% of the game's side quests are just three of these encounters chained together, each DLC is about 5 or 6 of these chained together but a little more fleshed out, and other side objectives that buff your stats in meaningful ways also require grinding these encounters; it's incredibly lazy. 

The main campaign is fine, but honestly not good enough for me to recommend. They don't make any meaningful improvements to the formula with [i]Tiny Tina's Wonderlands[/i] and the content is the laziest it has ever been. You're so much better off replaying [i]Borderlands 2[/i], or any Borderlands game for that matter. [i]Tiny Tina's Wonderlands[/i] is fine, but it doesn't stand out in the genre, or meet the bar of quality that I can recommend in this day and age. If you're buying it heavily discounted and have co-op partners to play with then it might be worth considering if you're really into these games, but otherwise just pass on it.

Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is, in my opinion, the most underrated and misunderstood Borderlands spinoff to date. Once you understand what the developers were going for, the whole experience clicks into place in a way that makes you appreciate just how creative and bold this game really is.

Let me explain the setup, because I think this is where a lot of people missed the point. The game is about Tiny Tina hanging out with her friends, playing a tabletop RPG called Bunkers & Badasses, their world's equivalent of Dungeons & Dragons. You aren't just a vault hunter in this one; you are one of Tina's friends sitting at the table. You create your character, and you play through the campaign alongside Tina and her crew. Once you understand that framing device, everything about the game's design suddenly makes sense. The developers weren't just making another Borderlands game; they were building a love letter to tabletop gaming, told through the chaotic, explosive lens of Tiny Tina. It's brilliant.

Gameplay-wise, it's what we know and love from any Borderlands game. You shoot, you loot, and you build your character into an absolute badass. The core loop is satisfying and familiar, but the fantasy setting adds a fresh coat of paint that keeps it feeling new. The story is silly—I mean, it's Tiny Tina, so of course it is—and it's genuinely funny throughout. The humor lands more often than not, and the chemistry between Tina and her friends at the table adds a layer of charm that the main series sometimes lacks.

Of course, the game isn't perfect, and it has its weak moments. The biggest one for me is traveling from region to region. The game has you physically move your character across a representation of the game board, and it can feel slow and tedious at times. It's not my favorite part of the experience, but I get why it's there. You're playing a board game, after all, and that movement is part of the tabletop simulation. I can respect the vision even if the execution doesn't always land for me.

Where the game really shines is in its variety. The enemy designs are creative, and the different themed regions—from mushroom forests to frozen peaks—keep things fresh and diverse throughout the campaign. The gun variety is a bit slow at the start, but it picks up significantly midway through your playthrough. Once you start finding legendary gear and experimenting with the multiclass system, the buildcrafting becomes some of the best in the entire series.

All in all, Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is a great time. It genuinely saddens me that Wonderlands 2 reportedly got canceled due to poor reception, because this game deserved a second chance to grow. It had so much potential, and it's a shame we might not see that vision expanded upon. But regardless of what could have been, this game is fun and definitely worth playing, especially if you're a Borderlands fan looking for something that dares to do things a little differently.

Give it a shot, and go in with the understanding that you're sitting down at Tina's table. You might just find yourself having a blast.

I really, really, really wanted to love this game. I have ~1500 hours in the Borderlands franchise across 4 platforms, and was very exited to see where the series was heading next. That said, I can't help but be disappointed. Things that Borderlands has been doing well for over a decade were changed, and not for the better.

The first change I found grating was the MMORPG style character creation system. While this is certainly a well designed and implemented system, one of the standout features of the Borderlands franchise has always been the player characters. The available character voices are very bland and boring. The remarks the player character makes become extremely predictable by the 2nd or 3rd hour. In previous entries, I was motivated to do at least one playthrough as every character, but this time around the characters (or classes) all feel very samey, despite the gameplay differences offered. Not to mention, the impact of action skills feels greatly reduced, going from gameplay defining to something more akin to a Destiny super ability. This is not to say they are not important in combat, and some skills impact playstyle more than others, but throwing a hammer or having two spells just doesn't feel the same as summoning a robot companion or going on a roided out ax rampage. Finally, the lack of individuality between player characters takes away from another major series highlight; the comedy writing.

Humor has been central to the design philosophy of the Borderlands franchise since its beginning. While Wonderlands has no shortage of attempts at humor, it really failed to resonate with me. While I understand that Wonderlands is attempting to depart slightly from the original Borderlands formula, the style of humor has shifted completely from a nihilistic and dry style to something more whimsical and childish. I feel this is mostly because this game is centered around Tiny Tina. While Tina was one of 12 year old me's favorite characters on my first few playthroughs of BL2, I feel we have had more than enough of her by now. About half of the NPCs are written solely to accommodate this new style of comedy, which severely  detracted from another franchise highlight. Almost all NPCs the player encounters are written to execute ONE joke, which is nothing new for Borderlands, but when the joke does not land it becomes annoying very quickly. Because of this, it is very difficult to care about the characters or the world they live in (more on this later). However, there are a few NPCs who are genuinely funny, and their scarcity almost makes them more enjoyable. Overall, this game's humor seems to be targeted at a middle school audience (perhaps explaining the T rating), but this leaves longtime (or adult) fans of the franchise left hanging. 

On the topic of Tiny Tina, making the story into a DnD campaign seriously took away from my interest in the story. Even in BL1, before the series' story or universe was fleshed out, you always felt like you were doing SOMETHING. There was a sense of purpose and real consequence to the story, whether trying to get rich or fighting to save the universe, the player had a reason to be slaughtering their way through the planet. Even in Tina's previous outing as a Dungeon Master, the player was tasked with helping Tina and the rest of the BL2 cast in dealing with the grief of losing a loved on and the overall toll the war on Hyperion has taken on them. This time around, the players motivation seemingly boils down to "We're bored, might as well play a board game to pass the time." Because of this, I found it extremely hard to invest in the story, as the outcome is extremely predictable, and the obstacles thrown at the player are little more than childish comic relief or heavy handed social commentary. Again, Borderlands is no stranger to either of these things, but too much of a good thing gets old pretty quick.

Finally, there are several gameplay features that really hurt the overall experience. The decision to remove convenient fast travel in exchange for a chibi-style overworld was especially tough to swallow, especially when said overworld is filled with random encounters and tedious, mandatory for progression fetch quests coupled with a painfully slow movement speed. While the added element of exploration is welcome, when the reward is a 5 minute arena combat segment only slightly different than the 5 you completed in the last hour or a series of collectibles combining into a negligible stat increase, exploring very quickly becomes more annoying than entertaining.

Another rather frustrating mechanic is the skill points system. While the time honored linear skill tree makes its return, it is accompanied by a secondary system similar to a FromSoft game. While these points can accumulate into very large buffs in the late game, you'll spend the early parts of your playthrough trying to get out of the negatives in the stats your background takes away from (this loss is unavoidable, there isn't an option to forgo the buffs and start with a clean slate). This system feels somewhat similar to BAR, but rather than being a reward for dedicated players, skill point min/maxing is essential for optimal late game builds. While this is certainly not a deal breaker, it makes build planning or switching all the more time consuming.

With all that said, there is still fun to be had in Wonderlands. The gunplay is fantastic, perhaps even better than BL3, and melee weapons are certainly a welcome addition. While the gun variety is somewhat lacking, what is available is unique (or at least gimicky) enough to keep things entertaining and add depth to combat beyond "click on head to do big damage." The action skills do blend into the combat fairly well despite their failings and can, at their worst, provide at the very least another button to click to kill things. 

Finally, there are some genuinely enjoyable characters and moments to be found in Wonderlands. The main antagonist is a shining example of the enigmatic villains Borderlands has been producing for years, and some jokes did get a laugh out of me. However, I still cannot recommend this game to a fan of the Borderlands games, at least not at full price. Wonderlands simply does not meet the standards set by even the Pre-Sequel, and this game as it stands is definitely not worth full price, or even the $48 sale price tag its currently sitting at.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? Yea, this isn't a bad little game, but, and this is a big but, my first playthrough was fun and enjoyable; everything was novel and intriguing, but going through things again quickly wore this feeling off and it became annoying. So, for me, the first playthrough is a positive experience, but after that, not so much it becomes meh. 

You can find typical Borderlands gameplay and some of the franchise's funny goofs here, but it isn't as good as the original Borderlands games, and the content and experience definitely drop off quickly. 

I definitely recommend waiting for a deep sale before purchasing this title, because the base price is not worth it.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
DLC is required for 100%. There are also two multiplayer achievements.  

You will need to do a minimum of 1 playthrough as well as the DLC and Chaos Chambers to get 100%. All of the achievements in the base game are pretty easy, just playing the game will net you most of them, the DLC missions that you need to run will need to be done a few times each. I recommend that you wait until the end to do these because doing one will unlock the weapons associated with it into the loot pool from now on, so if you're looking for something specific, I'd err on the side of caution before doing them; otherwise, they're not too bad. The chaos chambers are not particularly difficult and can be completed fairly easily, but having someone else to help will make it much easier.

The only real issue is the two final achievements for "unlocking all achievements" and "getting all the inventory upgrades."  The inventory upgrades are not cheap and will require an insane amount of money to get. Now there are ways around it, so if you value your time, there are ways around doing this massive boring grind. I will let you find them for yourself, but if you go for this fully legit, be prepared to drop a lot, and I mean a lot of hours, into this game. 

Aside from the inventory one, the rest are fine.

TLDR: awesome shooter in the classic looter shooter style of borderlands but with some refreshing additions along side a great cast and challenging endgame content!

It's been a wild ride playing this game, an interesting twist on the standard borderlands franchise which I've loved - the main characters being voiced by some of my favourite comedy actors (Will Arnett, Andy Samberg and Wanda Sykes) a great cast - if you love the dumb jokes all borderlands have you'll really enjoy this one - also adds some depth to Tina which hit close to home for me.

As for gameplay, it's nice to have a borderlands where you can customize your own hero even your classes too, yeh I get people aren't happy about the 3 trees but you pick your starting class then have a sub class which can make for some awesome synergies with which you can change once you finish the main story. 
For me it's great because you can really chop and change your playstyle on the fly/test out builds, really get into creating your own hero.

The spells in the game are a really nice addition aswell as the necklaces - it adds more to your builds, on normal BL you have your shields and mod but that's it, on TT it adds another layer which is more craziness. 

Each area has loot dice to find which ups your loot luck, I enjoyed finding them it really made you want to explore every nook and cranny of the maps and once you got all of them in all areas you got a beefy permanent boost to your luck.

The level cap is kind of low (40) you get to add attribute points each level up which makes it more like a classic RPG. The myth ranks at max level are nice, it still allows you to build on your character like badass rank but better imo as there's more bespoke options to really hone your builds.

The DLC I've been really enjoying, it's like 4 different multistage quests each having a main objective and an optional sub (which gives you more loot on each stage) enemies drop soul crystals which you spend to get loads of loot in the dlc hub area. 
The catch to each one is there's no save point, no checkpoints so you have to beat the whole thing to complete it - if you're playing with a buddy and they die they can't respawn until the other player has completed that stage of the mission, so if you die you're out until the next stage of the quest begins. 
You also can't leave or teleport out of a stage when you start a mission.
Each quest in the dlc after it's been beat adds another difficulty, up to difficulty 4 - I've only beaten tier 3 and it's been a real challenge.

At end game there's the chaos chamber, I've only just gotten that content unlocked and it's been really challenging so far - it even has secret bosses which honestly has kicked my ass! I breezed through the game on hard by my god the chaos levels really up the difficulty and push your builds to their limit. 
It's been awesome so far like a real new and refreshing addition to the game, curses, blessings, buffs, portals, crystals, puzzles, secret bosses, loot, EVERYTHING! 

Last point for me is the most important, you can have a mushroom boy who farts on enemies and revives you.... A. FUCKING. MUSHROOM. BOY. get this game....

Not sure why so many people complained about this game being too short, it took me over 40 hours to finish the story with still a few side quests to do and plenty of collectables left to gather. That's plenty of game and honestly it got a bit samey after a while anyway. After about halfway through you've pretty much seen all the enemy types in the game so the combat can get repetitive. That said it is also very fun if you're just after more Borderlands. The inclusion of spells is a nice change from grenades for the franchise, though I'll admit I pretty much used only 1 or 2 different spell types because having to hold down a button for several seconds looking at the point you want to cast a spell leaves you a vulnerable so got annoying. Good variety of classes and more interesting perk upgrades than usual.

Now the bad stuff. The game is way too easy. I rarely died and if I did it was because I missed a jump or accidentally bashed an exploding barrel thinking it was a regular one. Most boss fights were over within a matter of seconds with no strategy needed to defeat them. Ammo crates are spammed every 5 metres you walk so you never run out of ammo and have to change weapon so you only do so when you get bored. The UI is pretty poor. For example, to put a way point down on the map you think it would make sense that you could just click on the map where your mouse cursor is right? Well apparently not, because you have to drag your mouse across the screen to move the map cursor to the point on the map you want the way point to be. It's really awkward. Also the characters in the game apart from Tiny Tina are really lame and annoying. Not quite as bad as in BL3 but not far off. It was cringe inducing stuff.

There's a good game to be had, but the incessant chatter from cringey dialogue and laughably easy combat makes it easy to forget that the core gun play is the only thing holding this game together.

One of the standout aspects of this game is the ability to share loot, complete the story together, and engage in all side quests with friends. It offers a fun and engaging cooperative experience, making it an excellent choice for those looking to play with others while still enjoying a rich adventure.

However, one drawback is that purchasing all the DLCs is necessary to achieve 100% completion. Unfortunately, I found the DLCs to be quite expensive, which led me to skip buying them. Luckily, since my friend owned them, I was still able to experience the full game and earn all achievements. If you're playing with friends, this can be a great way to complete the game without each person having to buy all the DLCs. While the additional content does include some exciting boss fights, I personally don’t believe the price is justified. Ultimately, the DLCs are only essential for those who want to complete the game and wants 100% achievements.

Pros:
-Still has that solid gunplay flow from BL3, just fine tuned now with magic and mischief.
-There's even more QoL, enemy variety is fun, and the game has some great boss fights.
-The DND spirit is felt throughout this game.  From spells, npcs, overworld, or Tina's commentary throughout the game, Wonderlands is a love letter that beautifully blends the chaos of tabletop and Borderlands.
-Being able to create your own "fatemaker" feels fun with a ton of options to either make your dream hero or a complete monstrosity.  The build diversity alongside gives you several options to slay baddies.
-This is the best story since Anthony Burch's departure.  The Dragon Lord is a great villain, and there is a fun whimsy to the game's tone that is uplifting and charming.
-I LOVE the Chaos Chamber.  Your mileage may vary with this mode, but it's great to jump in at any time to face a dungeon full of enemies.

Cons:
-My primary critique is that the season pass (even on sale) is still massively overpriced for what it is.  Unless you REALLY like the chaos chamber, you aren't missing that much by skipping it.  Hopefully, we get some legitimate one-shot expansions down the line.
-Nitpicky, but the music is more atmospheric then the bombastic sonic you're used to with Borderlands and I miss it here.  Your preference in tone will determine how you feel on this one though.

Final Note:
To those who waited, whenever you jump into Wonderlands, you will have a blast alone or with friends!

✔️ Nice iteration over the Borderlands formula in a kinda medieval fantasy setting.
✔️ Cool spell system that replaces the grenades from other Borderlands games, enjoyable alternative gameplay that uses cooldowns instead of ammo.

💭 The fact player characters don't have any specific personality removes a lot from their charisma. On the other hand it allows the players to be fully in control of what they imagine for those, but it kinda breaks off with part of what tends to make the Borderlands experience impactful.
💭 The overworld feature is a bit of a mediocre addition - in theory the idea seems nice and fun, but it makes movements between areas a bit more tedious in the way it is implemented, while obfuscating a bunch of features in UI behind several layers of menus (we only discovered we could fast travel to non-Brighthoof areas near the end of the game for instance).
💭 The overall narration is... pretty meh. Nothing awful, but where the Dragonkeep DLC for Borderlands 2 explored Tina's way to process her emotions, Wonderlands tries to do the same, but misses the point by not actually engaging with any powerful emotions aside from a few glimpses of abandonment issues. It prefers focusing more on a lighthearted and chill tabletop RPG story rather than poking into more serious subjects, while in my opinion the mix of the fun and the serious is what generally makes Borderlands stories compelling.
💭 The post-game feels a bit poor and repetitive. Not a big issue if you don't plan on lingering after the main story end, but it's just empty procedural content with little to no actual progression or matter to explore.

❌ The random encounters and similar stuff sucks pretty hard. The fact the random encounter arenas are often the same, not very interactive, and don't have any loot or narrative purpose, in addition to not having a minimap, makes them really feel like the dumb fillers they are.
